title: Article 4 — Laws under Articles 2 and 3 to provide for amendment of the First and Fourth Schedules and supplemental matters

content.overview: Article 4 provides that any law referred to in Article 2 or Article 3 shall contain such provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the law and may also contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions as Parliament may deem necessary. Clause (2) declares that no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.
content.glance: Laws under Arts 2/3 may amend First & Fourth Schedules + supplemental provisions. Such laws are NOT Article 368 amendments.
content.study:
Article 4 is the machinery clause that makes Articles 2 and 3 effective without triggering the special amendment procedure of Article 368.

Clause (1): A law under Article 2 or 3 —
- shall contain such provisions for amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule as are necessary to give effect to the law; and
- may contain supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (e.g. representation in Parliament, allocation of seats, transitional administration, adaptation of laws).

Clause (2): No such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.

Consequence: State reorganisation and admission/establishment laws pass by ordinary parliamentary majority (subject to the Article 3 proviso on Presidential recommendation and State reference). They do not require the special majorities or ratification process of Article 368.

Fourth Schedule: allocation of seats in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha). Reorganisation typically requires consequential changes to Rajya Sabha seat allocation, which Article 4 expressly permits.

sections.heading: Constitutional text (substance)
sections.body:
(1) Any law referred to in Article 2 or Article 3 shall contain such provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the law and may also contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to representation in Parliament and in the Legislature or Legislatures of the State or States affected by such law) as Parliament may deem necessary.
(2) No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.

sections.heading: Why Article 4 matters
sections.body: Without Article 4, every change to the First Schedule (list of States/UTs) or Fourth Schedule (Rajya Sabha seats) might be argued to require a formal constitutional amendment. Article 4 avoids that result and keeps territorial reorganisation within ordinary legislative power, subject only to the procedural safeguards in Article 3.

sections.heading: Exam checkpoints
sections.body:
1. Quote both clauses.
2. First Schedule + Fourth Schedule amendments authorised.
3. Supplemental/incidental/consequential provisions allowed (including parliamentary representation).
4. Explicitly: not an Article 368 amendment.
5. Link back to Articles 2 and 3 as the source powers.

examples.title: Illustration — Reorganisation Act
examples.body: A States Reorganisation Act under Article 3 amends the First Schedule (new State entries), amends the Fourth Schedule (Rajya Sabha seats), and provides for sitting members, assets, and adaptation of laws. Article 4 sustains all of these elements and confirms that the Act is not an Article 368 amendment.

misconceptions.trap: Changing the First Schedule always requires an Article 368 amendment.
misconceptions.correction: When the change is effected by a law under Article 2 or 3, Article 4 provides that it is not an amendment for the purposes of Article 368.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the effect of Article 4?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Article 4 provides that laws under Articles 2 and 3 shall contain necessary amendments to the First and Fourth Schedules and may contain supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including as to representation). Clause (2) declares that no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368. Thus territorial reorganisation and admission/establishment of States proceed by ordinary legislation, not the special amendment procedure.

examTips: Always state clause (2): not an Art 368 amendment. Mention both First and Fourth Schedules.

Such laws are not Art 368 amendments.
